hooks.text: Every star in the universe will eventually go out forever.
In 100 trillion years, all star formation permanently ends.
Even giant black holes will eventually evaporate into pure darkness.

title: When the Last Black Hole Explodes
description: In the deep future of our universe, star formation will completely halt and even supermassive black holes will evaporate away. Here is how the cosmos reaches its dark final era.

beats.text: Every star in the universe will eventually go out forever.
beats.visual: Hubble eXtreme Deep Field showing thousands of distant galaxies, 2012

beats.text: All interstellar gas will run dry in about 100 trillion years.
beats.visual: Artist's impression of a low-mass red dwarf star, 2017
queries: Red dwarf star ESO artist impression

beats.text: The last remaining red dwarfs will slowly fade into dark black dwarfs.
beats.visual: Hubble image of the Ring Nebula surrounding a cooling white dwarf, 2013

beats.text: Gravitational encounters will then fling most dead stars into deep space.
beats.visual: Hubble image of the Antennae Galaxies colliding and exchanging stars, 2006

beats.text: Only supermassive black holes will remain in the empty void.
beats.visual: Event Horizon Telescope shadow image of supermassive black hole Messier 87, 2019
queries: Messier 87 black hole Event Horizon Telescope
Sagittarius A star Event Horizon Telescope

beats.text: Yet even black holes lose mass through quantum Hawking radiation.
beats.visual: Diagram depicting Hawking radiation escaping a black hole event horizon, 2015

beats.text: Until even supermassive black holes detonate and evaporate away.
beats.visual: Artist concept of a dying black hole exploding in a final radiation burst, 2020

beats.text: That leaves behind a frozen cosmos where no new light can ever ignite.
beats.visual: Planck spacecraft all-sky map of the cosmic microwave background radiation, 2018
